signals.title: llm-d 1.0, an open source stack for distributed inference | Google Cloud Blog
signals.excerpt:
llm-d 1.0, an open source stack for distributed inference | Google Cloud Blog

October 20, 2026

##### Mark Lohmeyer

Product Manager

##### Nov 4: Agentic Data Cloud Event

Today at the PyTorch Conference, we released llm-d 1.0, an open-source, Kubernetes-native stack for distributed LLM inference. Co-founded by Google with Red Hat, IBM and others, we worked with a community of more than 500 contributors over 25 organizations on this Cloud Native Computing Foundation (CNCF) Sandbox project, bringing together two important communities: PyTorch, where vLLM and SGLang serve models, and Kubernetes, where distributed systems run and scale in production.

...

### What 1.0 provides

llm-d already delivered prefix- and load-aware routing, KV cache offloading, prefill/decode disaggregation, wide expert parallelism and batch inference across Google Cloud TPUs and GPUs. These capabilities provide:

- Multi-tenant quality of service. Priority and fairness-aware routing via llm-d flow control, helping latency-sensitive requests and bursty agent workloads share a fleet to meet SLOs without starving one another.
- A stable foundation. v1 APIs and a hardened request path, validated on multiple clouds and accelerator types.
- Safer upgrades. Router high availability and zero-downtime updates, alongside DisaggregatedSet, which orchestrates prefill/decode-aware rolling updates without dropping context or disrupting active sessions.
- Agent-aware serving. Session-aware routing, turn-priority scheduling, and native Responses API state, helping agents reuse context across turns.
- Expanded TPU integration. Native PyTorch model serving with TorchTPU co-operative time-slicing to raise throughput and utilization across Google Cloud TPU fleets.

The components are designed so that you can compose them into your own bespoke production environment. Keep your engine, model and cluster, and adopt only the serving components and configurations you need.

...

On an agentic coding workload on Ironwood TPU (TPU 7x), prefix-aware routing plus host memory offload cut median time-to-first-token (TTFT) by more than 85% and raised total throughput 2.4x versus a plain Kubernetes Service, as of October 2026 (source).

...

During RL training, accelerators often sit idle 40% to 60% of the time during rollout generation or weight updates. llm-d now supports Google Cloud TPU and GPU time-slicing to interleave async inference into those quiet cycles, raising aggregate accelerator duty cycles from a ~40% baseline to >70% (source).

Benchmarks you can trust

Tuning a distributed inference stack across routers, KV cache tiers, and prefill/decode pools takes repeatable measurement under realistic multi-turn load. Prism is llm-d’s open-source analysis dashboard for exploring published benchmarks across llm-d’s well-lit paths, backed by standardized llm-d-benchmark recipes and inference-perf workloads. Inspect the exact configurations behind the numbers, or upload runs from your own cluster to compare throughput, latency, and cost curves side by side.

...

### In production

This GKE llm-d stack carries production traffic, and it has been tested at fleet scale:

- Gemini platform (formerly Vertex AI) serves production traffic through GKE Inference Gateway, doubling its prefix cache hit rate from 35% to 70%, cutting TTFT by more than 35% for coding agents and cutting P95 TTFT by more than 50% under bursty chat traffic (source).
- In a published benchmark across a 17,000-node multi-region GKE deployment serving a mixture-of-experts model in the US and Europe, multi-cluster GKE Inference Gateway and the llm-d router scaled throughput 2.9x across three clusters with a 99.9% success rate and less than 1% routing overhead (source).
- In a published benchmark on A3 Mega cluster serving a 70B-parameter model, llm-d with multi-connector KV cache offloading to Google Cloud Managed Lustre in addition to Host CPU RAM, delivered an approximately 40% improvement in TTFT and a 30% reduction in end-to-end latency responding to 50k-token prompts compared to CPU RAM offload only, while reducing GPU-hour requirements by nearly 60% (source).

...

### Get started

1. Check out the full demo of llm-d with TPUs at the Google Cloud booth during the PyTorch Conference.
2. Deploy llm-d 1.0 on GKE with the verified Helm charts. See the llm-d on GKE documentation.
3. Start with prefix-aware routing in front of your existing vLLM deployment, then add flow control, KV cache offload (SGlang, vLLM) and disaggregation.
4. Compare results on Prism and contribute on GitHub.

signals.title: Announcing Humming: Fast, Flexible Kernels for Quantized Inference | vLLM Blog
signals.excerpt:
Announcing Humming: Fast, Flexible Kernels for Quantized Inference | vLLM Blog

# Announcing Humming: Fast, Flexible Kernels for Quantized Inference

October 21, 2026 19 min read

Table of Contents

Ant Group and the vLLM community are open-sourcing Humming, a general-purpose, high-performance kernel library for quantized inference. Humming offers the following features:

- Broad device support: Supports NVIDIA GPU architectures from Turing onward, along with CUDA-compatible devices such as T-Head's Zhenwu 810E.
- Extensive quantization support: A unified architecture supports diverse combinations of weight and activation formats for dense and MoE workloads, covering a wide range of integer and floating-point types, bit widths, and scaling schemes.
- Strong execution performance: Significantly outperforms existing implementations from vLLM Marlin, FlashInfer, and DeepGEMM across many representative workloads.

Repository: github.com/vllm-project/humming

...

As models and inference workloads grow, memory capacity, memory bandwidth, and compute costs increasingly constrain deployment. This is especially apparent in MoE models: each token activates only a subset of experts, but the full set of weights still needs to be stored. DeepSeek-V3, for example, has 671 billion parameters, with 37 billion activated per token. Quantization lowers the precision of weights and activations to reduce memory usage and data movement, and can also improve compute efficiency.

Quantization requirements vary across models and GPU generations. Common configurations include WNA16, W8A8, W4A8, and W4A4, where W and A specify weight and activation bit widths, and N denotes a variable weight bit width. Even at the same precision, schemes such as INT4 and NVFP4 differ in numeric format and scaling. Scaling granularity, scale representation, group size, and symmetric or asymmetric quantization further expand the configuration space.

These storage and compute savings only translate into lower latency and higher throughput with efficient kernels. Prefill, decode, and varying MoE expert loads place different demands on compute and memory. Kernels must adapt to these workloads while keeping conversion, dequantization, and scheduling overhead low.

...

## General-Purpose Architecture

Humming's execution path has three parts: represent the quantized computation, select configurations for the hardware and workload, and compile a kernel from CUDA components.

...

### Broad Device Support

Humming's unified architecture enables broad GPU support. For NVIDIA GPUs, Humming fully supports every architecture from Turing onward, bringing a common quantized computing framework to multiple generations of hardware.

The unified JIT architecture also makes it straightforward to extend Humming to other GPUs compatible with CUDA programming. Humming already fully supports T-Head's Zhenwu 810E, bringing its shared kernels and tuning capabilities to more hardware platforms.

...

#### End-to-End Inference Performance

Humming's W4A8 gains extend to model serving. In our DeepSeek-V4.1-Flash test on eight H20 GPUs with TP=8, keeping the model's MXFP4 weights unchanged and switching MoE execution from Marlin W4A16 (BF16 activations) to Humming W4A8 (tokenwise FP8 activations) improves end-to-end throughput by approximately 14%–43% and reduces mean time to first token (TTFT) by approximately 25%–32%. The throughput advantage grows with concurrency: at concurrency 64, output throughput rises from 442.37 to 633.94 tokens/s, while mean time per output token (TPOT) falls by approximately 31%.

Announcing New vLLM and SGLang Inference Engines on TPU
            
            
            - Google Developers Blog
signals.excerpt:
Announcing New vLLM and SGLang Inference Engines on TPU - Google Developers Blog 

# Announcing New vLLM and SGLang Inference Engines on TPU

OCT. 20, 2026

 Qi Zhou Principal Software Engineer 

 Chris Chan Group Product Manager 

As part of our broader announcements for PyTorch today, we are excited to launch native PyTorch backends for vLLM (developed in partnership with Inferact) and SGLang (developed in partnership with RadixArk).

## Background

For years, TPUs have powered large-scale AI workloads with high performance and efficiency. With the rise of agentic and multimodal workloads, serving efficiently is more important than ever. vLLM and SGLang already run on TPU through JAX-based backend, but we kept hearing from developers that they wanted to customize and debug their serving stack in PyTorch.

So we started in earnest on TorchTPU, which runs PyTorch natively on TPU. We then built new vLLM and SGLang engines on top of it.

Our goal is for the PyTorch community to bring models to TPU and make them fast using the tools developers are already familiar with. The engines come with optimized, production-ready serving features and custom Pallas kernels.

...

### Workload support

Both engines are built for the full range of production workloads.

Here’s the list of supported features:

- Agentic & Multi-Turn: Automatic prefix caching, including for hybrid models; KV cache offloading to host memory and Managed Lustre through TPU Sync; tool calling and structured output
- Interactive & Low Latency: Speculative decoding with MTP, EAGLE-3, DFlash, DSpark and n-gram drafters
- High-throughput Batch: Data-parallel attention with expert parallelism
- Long Context: Context parallelism for prefill and decode; FP8 KV cache; host KV offloading
- Disaggregated Serving: Prefill and decode on separate hosts over TPU Sync, including between different parallel layouts
- Multimodal: Vision-language models with image and video input; embedding models
- Very Large Models: Hybrid and sparse-attention architectures, tensor, data, expert, pipeline and context parallelism across hosts; FP8, FP4 (MXFP4, NVFP4), INT8 and INT4 checkpoints

...

## Running today in production & public benchmarks

Both engines are already running at scale in production with preview customers. To provide transparent, reproducible proof of our performance, we benchmark in public through the community-standard SemiAnalysis InferenceX project.

Building on our initial submission of Qwen 3.5 on Ironwood TPU (TPU 7x), our engineering teams have further optimized the stack, bringing the lowest cost per million tokens overall to an industry leading 2.01 cents. Alongside these improvements, we have also published new state-of-the-art (SOTA) performance results to AgentX, the project's dedicated track for evaluating agentic long-context and multi-turn workloads. Ironwood TPU leads across most of the Pareto frontier. We look forward to continuously updating our public performance profiles as we bring more models and configurations to the leaderboard.

signals.title: Introducing vLLM TorchTPU | vLLM Blog
signals.excerpt:
# Introducing vLLM TorchTPU

October 20, 2026 6 min read

Table of Contents

Today we're releasing vLLM TorchTPU (`vllm-torchtpu`), a new backend for running vLLM on Google Cloud TPUs. It's built on Google's TorchTPU stack and runs the model definitions that already live in vLLM, so most models that work in vLLM today can be served on TPU without changes to the model code.

This work comes out of the engineering partnership between Inferact and Google we announced last month. Our goals for the project are to:

1. Make it easy to bring new models to TPU by reusing vLLM's existing model code.
2. Push TPU inference performance in open source, with Pallas kernels for attention, Mixture-of-Experts, and quantized matmul.
3. Keep the vLLM experience the same: the same CLI, OpenAI-compatible server, scheduler, and KV cache manager you use on other hardware.

...

### How It Works

`vllm-torchtpu` is an out-of-tree vLLM platform plugin. Once installed, vLLM picks it up automatically through the `vllm.platform_plugins` entry point.

Models run through vLLM's standard model runner and are compiled with `torch.compile(backend="tpu")`, which lowers to XLA. Each TPU device gets its own worker process, the same way vLLM runs on GPUs, and communication between devices goes through `torch.distributed`. This means the scheduler, workers, KV cache manager, and API server are all unmodified upstream vLLM. The TPU-specific work sits underneath them, mostly in a set of JAX/Pallas kernels that are registered as custom ops and called from inside the compiled graph.

...

### Kernels

`vllm-torchtpu` uses custom Pallas kernels for complex operations that benefit from hand-tuning on TPU. Some examples:

- Ragged Paged Attention v3 for MHA/GQA models
- Dense and sparse Multi-head Latent Attention (MLA) for DeepSeek, Kimi, and GLM
- Gated DeltaNet and Kimi Delta Attention for hybrid linear-attention models
- Fused Mixture-of-Experts with expert parallelism
- FP8, INT8, MXFP4, and NVFP4 quantized matmuls

...

### Models, Features, and What's Next

`vllm-torchtpu` can serve most models supported by vLLM, with TPU-specific kernel, quantization, and parallelism work for the Qwen, DeepSeek, Kimi, GLM, Llama, GPT-OSS, and Gemma families. TPU v7x (Ironwood) is the recommended hardware and is tested in CI on every pull request; v6e, v5e, and v5p are experimental.

The Supported Models & Features page has the full list of validated checkpoints and features, with how to enable each one. The nightly support matrices track TPU v7x correctness and benchmark results from CI.

signals.title: ByteDance's OpenViking agent context database hits 40,000 GitHub stars
signals.excerpt:
# ByteDance's OpenViking agent context database hits 40,000 GitHub stars

OpenViking from ByteDance's Volcengine treats agent memory, knowledge and skills as a virtual filesystem, crossing 40,000 GitHub stars.

 By Marcello Babbili · AI-assisted newsroom October 19, 2026 3 min read 

Image generated by OpenAI

ByteDance's Volcengine team published OpenViking, an open-source context database that treats everything an AI agent knows as files under a `viking://` filesystem, and the project crossed 40,000 stars on GitHub this week after gaining 105 stars in a single day on the platform's trending list S¹.

The approach challenges how most agent builders work today: stitching together separate systems for retrieval-augmented generation (the standard method for feeding documents into a model), conversation memory, and tool or skill management. OpenViking collapses all three into one virtual filesystem that an agent can browse and read on demand P² P⁴.

...

### One filesystem, three context types

The Viking team, part of ByteDance's cloud infrastructure arm Volcengine, organises context into three types: resources for reference material, memories for information retained from interactions, and skills for task procedures P⁴. Each piece of context loads in three tiers: L0, a one-sentence abstract; L1, a core overview; and L2, the full original data S¹. An agent scans the L0 summaries to decide what it needs, then drills down to L2 only for relevant items, which keeps token consumption down.

When a conversation session ends, OpenViking commits and archives it as Markdown files that a developer can read and edit by hand S¹. Memories sit in readable text, not a binary store, which makes debugging and correction straightforward.

...

### The benchmarks nobody has checked

The project reports evaluation results on two benchmarks: LoCoMo, which tests long-conversation user memory, and tau2-bench, which tests multi-turn agent tasks S¹. Version 0.3.22 used Doubao 2.0 Pro, Volcengine's own vision-language model, for the memory evaluation S¹. These results are self-reported. The repository does not include peer-reviewed or third-party-audited benchmark data, and the README is the maintainers' description of their own work, not an independent review.

A developer who wants to try the system without committing to an install can use OpenViking Studio, a browser-based demo that requires no setup S¹.

The repository is written primarily in Python and carries the volcengine organisation label on GitHub, though the about page confirms the team sits inside ByteDance's Volcengine unit P².

Until an independent team reproduces the LoCoMo or tau2-bench results, the 40,000-star count measures interest, not proof.

signals.title: EmbeddingGemma 2 Expands Beyond Text to Support Code, Images, Video, and Audio - InfoQ
signals.excerpt:
Oct 19, 2026 2 min read 

by

- Sergio De Simone 

Based on Gemma 4 and released under the Apache 2.0 license, Google's EmbeddingGemma 2 is a compact, open-weight, multimodal embedding model designed to make semantic search and retrieval-augmented generation (RAG) more efficient while optimizing performance for on-device deployment.

> Designed to run on consumer hardware such as mobile devices and laptops, EmbeddingGemma 2 delivers low-latency semantic representations for on-device applications, like search, retrieval-augmented generation (RAG), classification, and clustering.

Thanks to its multimodal capabilities, EmbeddingGemma 2 supports a wide range of retrieval tasks, including finding relevant documents, screenshots, and recordings in response to a query, searching source code using natural language, and retrieving video content based on textual descriptions.

EmbeddingGemma 2's key feature, Google says, is its ability to represent text, code, images, video, and audio in a unified 768-dimensional embedding space. This enables developers to build retrieval systems that search across different media types without maintaining separate, incompatible embedding spaces for different media types.

> Despite coming from different modalities, the embeddings generated by EmbeddingGemma 2 occupy the same dimensional space and can be compared on their semantic similarity.

The model allows developers to load only the encoders required for their applications, scaling from 270 million parameters for text and code to 740 million for full multimodal support. According to Google, the model "significantly outperforms EmbeddingGemma 1 on code search and technical retrieval, making it ideal for local codebase indexing and agentic code search".

...

EmbeddingGemma 2 supports Matryoshka Representation Learning (MRL), which allows embeddings to be truncated into shorter, unit-length vectors, reducing storage requirements. For example, storing a million 768-dimensional vectors at bfloat16 precision takes roughly 1.5 GB of memory, while truncating them to 128 dimensions requires just 250 MB, bringing a sixfold reduction. However, this implies a retrieval quality trade-off. Google therefore recommends using truncation only when storage or search speed require it. At 128 dimensions, the model retains approximately 90% of quality with text, but performance drops to around 75% for image, video, and speech retrieval.

...

EmbeddingGemma was introduced last year with a focus on "offline and privacy-sensitive scenarios, such as searching across personal files locally, running mobile RAG pipelines with Gemma 3n, or building domain-specific chatbots". EmbeddingGemma 2 is available on Hugging Face.

signals.title: Crossing the threshold to dependable open source AI serving
signals.excerpt:
When large open weight models first captured attention, the industry was faced with a challenge. Powerful open models were becoming available, but technologists lacked an open inference serving system that could run them efficiently. Having spent years building inference engines for CPUs, my team and I redirected all of our energy toward the vLLM project. Together with the community, vLLM capabilities expanded to become the de facto inference server. Today the vLLM project, now part of the PyTorch foundation, has a vibrant community of companies and developers actively adding support for new models, hardware, and research techniques.

As Red Hat continued this work, conversations with our enterprise users exposed a new reality. Getting a single server to perform efficiently was table stakes. The next challenge was orchestrating model serving at cluster scale. Last spring, we announced the llm-d project to address this, developing an open source, Kubernetes-native orchestration layer for distributed LLM serving across multi-tenant production clusters. Today, Red Hat and our community partners announced the release of llm-d 1.0. Reaching this milestone reflects a project hitting full maturity, shaped by hardened code, stability proven under real production load, and widespread adoption across an expanding contributor community. Open source AI serving has crossed from an experimental science project into dependable infrastructure you can build on.

...

Stability cannot be established on synthetic benchmarks alone. It has to survive real-world scale where agent contexts expand over hours of execution and accelerator memory faces unrelenting pressure. When multi-turn workloads repeatedly hit unmanaged clusters, naive load balancers scatter requests, wiping out cached prefix state and triggering massive recomputation costs.

llm-d delivers production-scale stability by making the orchestration layer aware of inference dynamics. It preserves context locality, disaggregates prefill from decode phases, and balances work across heterogeneous accelerator pools. In production, this operational stability creates dramatic efficiencies. At IBM Research, exploring quantum error correction hardware on llm-d generated multi-turn workloads with massive context reuse identical to agentic coding loops. That deployment yielded a 98% prefix-cache hit rate and reduced blended serving costs five to ten times compared to proprietary options.

In benchmark demonstrations, researchers used llm-d to deploy GLM-5.2, an approximately 753-billion-parameter open weight model on widely deployed NVIDIA GPUs, showcasing how enterprises can use existing GPU fleets to serve frontier-class AI at scale. On a workload with hundreds of agentic sessions running in parallel, llm-d delivered over 6.6 million output tokens per minute at peak on agentic benchmarks. The cluster sustained up to 3,000 concurrent coding agents with zero preemptions, demonstrating that llm-d can efficiently serve large mixture-of-experts models for agentic workloads.

signals.title: EAGLE 4 on AMD Instinct GPUs
signals.excerpt:
EAGLE 4 on AMD Instinct GPUs

# EAGLE-4 on AMD Instinct GPUs from day 0

 Oct 20, 2026

EAGLE-4, the newest drafter from the EAGLE team, runs on AMD Instinct™ MI355X GPUs from day 0, in SGLang and ATOM. - On Qwen3.8-27B, one MI355X GPU serves a single request at ~300 tokens/s in BF16: 3.5x plain decoding and 1.6x the model’s built-in MTP. - The gain holds as load grows, from 1 to 32 concurrent conversations, and scales to four GPUs. It works out of the box: the same checkpoint and the same serving flags as on other hardware.

...

## What is new in EAGLE-4

Speculative decoding lets a small drafter guess several tokens ahead, and the large model checks them all in one pass. EAGLE-4 adds three ideas on top of the EAGLE family:

- One drafter for every batch size and every GPU. EAGLE-4 drafts one token at a time, so it can stop, deepen or widen its guess tree at every step. EAGLE-Harness measures what drafting and verifying cost on the actual hardware, once at start-up. During serving it picks the tree that gives the most accepted tokens per unit of cost: a wide, deep tree for a single user, short chains under heavy load.
- A cheaper LM head for the drafter. The drafter’s vocabulary projection used to be most of its cost. A low-rank head first shortlists candidates from the full vocabulary, then the full head scores only those exactly. This cuts the draft’s cost by more than 40% without truncating the vocabulary.
- A small drafter. One transformer layer, so it fits next to the model with little memory, from data-center GPUs down to edge devices.

...

## Day 0 on AMD Instinct GPUs

EAGLE-4 runs on the MI355X GPU with the same checkpoint and the same launch flags as elsewhere:

To make it fast on day 0, we measured EAGLE-Harness’s cost tables on the MI355X GPU, so tree sizes fit this GPU; added tree verification for Qwen3.8’s linear-attention (Gated DeltaNet) layers: a guess tree is checked in one pass, and only the accepted branch’s state is kept; checked losslessness: every output token matches plain decoding, up to BF16 rounding at near-ties.

signals.title: Muse Spark Open on Fireworks: Meta’s Open Weights Model, Available on US Serverless
signals.excerpt:
Muse Spark Open on Fireworks: Meta’s Open Weights Model, Available on US Serverless

# Muse Spark Open on Fireworks: Meta’s open weights wodel, available on US serverless

PUBLISHED 10/20/2026

Muse Spark Open, an open weights model from Meta, is available Day-0 on Fireworks. It's an 816B-parameter mixture-of-experts model with 42B parameters active per token and a 1M-token context window, built for long-horizon coding and agent work that has to stay coherent across very long sessions.

It’s one of the most capable US open weights model to date, and the strongest open weights model we’ve seen for regulated professional work. It ranks first on Vals AI’s leaderboard for Harvey’s Legal Agent Benchmark, with nearly 4x the pass rate of Claude Opus 5. On Rogo’s Big Finance Bench, it beat Claude Opus 5.5 at every difficulty level and edged out GPT-6 Astra on the hardest tasks.

Muse Spark Open was trained and developed in the US, and Fireworks runs it with Zero Data Retention by default. Try it today on serverless, running on US-only capacity with no US premium. Then move to reserved throughput for production and fine-tune it with serverless LoRA training.

...

## Muse Spark Open outperforms Claude Opus on regulated work

Muse Spark Open does its best work where accuracy is paramount, such as legal, finance, and clinical tasks. These results come from independent evaluators and our Specialized Intelligence Index, where every model runs on the same harness:

- •#1 on Harvey’s egal Agent Benchmark: On Vals AI’s leaderboard for completing legal work with files and tools, Muse Spark Open ranks first of 75 models at 25.4%, nearly 4x Claude Opus 5 (6.7%).
- • Ahead of Claude Opus 5.5 on Rogo’s Big Finance Bench: In Fireworks’ Specialized Intelligence Index runs, Muse Spark Open beat Claude Opus 5.5 at every difficulty level. On the hardest tasks, it edged out GPT-6 Astra (17.3% vs. 16.5%) and scored more than 2.5x Opus 5.5 (6.6%) (Figure 1).
- • Top three on Finance Agent: On Vals AI’s Finance Agent v2, it scored 60.6%, within a point of Gemini 3.8 Flash at about 60% lower cost per test.
- • Clinical documentation: It scored 90.1% on Vals MedScribe, within a point of Claude Opus 5 (91.0%), at 75-83% lower token prices.

Third-party results from Vals AI and Artificial Analysis in this post were measured on Meta’s API release of this model.

...

## How Muse Spark Open scores on standard benchmarks

Muse Spark Open holds its own on standard public benchmarks:

- • Fewer hallucinations: On Artificial Analysis’ AA-Omniscience, it has a 33% hallucination rate, lower than Claude Opus 5.5 (59%) and GPT-6 Astra (51%), because it declines to answer when unsure instead of guessing.
- • Agentic coding: In Meta's evaluations, it scores 82.9% on Terminal-Bench 2.1, ahead of GPT-5.6 Terra and Grok 4.5 (Figure 2).

## Abstract

We introduce Muse Glimmer, an open-source 30B parameter causal language model with perception encoder, purpose-built for autonomous agentic tasks on consumer hardware. signals.title: RuVector: Self-Learning Vector Database for AI Agent Memory
signals.excerpt:
# Cognitum One Launches Commercial RuVector, the Self-Learning Database Giving AI Agents Memory That Persists, Connects and Improves

Tuesday, 20 October 2026 09:50 AM

#### Product Announcements

The open-source Rust engine combines vector search, graph relationships and self-learning memory, now backed by Cognitum One commercial licensing, enterprise support and deployment services.

SAN FRANCISCO, CA / ACCESS Newswire / October 20, 2026 / AI agents forget. Each session starts from scratch, context is lost between tasks, and most vector databases store embeddings without recording how ideas connect or which answers proved useful. Cognitum One ™, Inc. (cognitum.one) today launched RuVector ™ commercially, adding licensing, enterprise support and deployment services to the open-source project. RuVector is an open-source Rust engine that combines vector search, graph relationships and self-learning memory for AI agents. It runs in PostgreSQL, in the browser and at the edge, so memory can sit wherever an organization's data and agents already are.

RuVector has a large developer base behind it: more than 500,000 downloads a month across its npm and crates.io packages as of September 30, 2026, plus more than 4,400 GitHub stars and 580 forks. Within Cognitum One's platform, the roles are distinct. Ruflo coordinates teams of agents, ruOS gives them governed computers, and RuVector is what they remember.

...

What RuVector Does

- Search and relationships in one engine. Fast vector search (HNSW indexing with SIMD acceleration, sub-millisecond queries) works alongside a Cypher-compatible knowledge graph. An agent can find similar material and follow how facts relate without a second database.
- Improves retrieval from explicitly recorded feedback. When teams record which results helped, SONA updates lightweight LoRA adapters, and EWC++ consolidation protects earlier learning. Reads alone never change learned weights. Adapter learning is separate from index tuning and ranking settings, which teams control directly.
- Works inside PostgreSQL. The ruvector-postgres extension is pgvector-compatible and adds 143 SQL functions for vector, graph and hybrid search inside an existing database. Teams should confirm compatibility for their specific pgvector workloads; full migration details are in the technical guide.
- Signed, portable memory. The RVF file format packages vectors, indexes and metadata in a single file with copy-on-write branching and SHAKE256 witness chains, a tamper-evident record of every change. The same memory runs on servers, in WebAssembly in the browser and on edge devices, and running locally avoids hosted vector-service fees.

...

Why RuVector Stands Apart

RuVector extends conventional retrieval-augmented generation (RAG) by combining similarity search with graph relationships, persistent agent memory and learning from explicitly recorded feedback. It brings these capabilities together in one Rust engine for AI agents, RAG and intelligence workflows.

- It learns instead of just storing. Traditional vector databases are passive storage. RuVector adds a graph neural network layer between initial search and final results that strengthens frequently used paths, and Cognitum One reports accuracy gains of 10 to 30 percent from usage feedback. SONA applies continuous LoRA micro-updates on a standard CPU, with Elastic Weight Consolidation protecting earlier learning from catastrophic forgetting.
- A tech stack in a box. One engine replaces several systems: HNSW vector search, a graph engine with Cypher queries and hyperedges, and ruvllm, a built-in local runtime that runs language models and generates embeddings on-device with CUDA and Metal acceleration. An RVF file can bundle data, models and graph structures into a single artifact that boots a microkernel in milliseconds, making RuVector work almost like an operating system for agents at the edge.
- Performance built in Rust. Production Rust with SIMD (AVX-512 and NEON) delivers search latency as low as 61 microseconds, which Cognitum One's benchmarks put at 30 to 800 times faster than typical vector databases, and more than 52,000 inserts per second on commodity hardware.
- A fraction of the memory. RuVector needs about 200 MB of memory per million vectors, compared with the 1 to 3 GB typical of other vector databases. Automated RaBitQ and product quantization compress data 2 to 32 times, so demanding workloads run on low-cost CPUs without GPUs.
- Zero-config, everywhere. A single npm install ruvector detects the system and uses native Rust bindings, or falls back to WebAssembly for browsers and iOS. The PostgreSQL extension brings the same self-learning search to existing relational workflows.

...

Availability

RuVector is available today. The core project remains open source under the MIT license. A Cognitum One commercial license adds a contract with enterprise support, deployment and configuration services, upgrade and maintenance commitments, and deployment with Ruflo ™ and ruOS ™ on infrastructure the customer controls. Model and infrastructure costs still apply.

Cognitum One recommends starting with one memory store and one agent, measuring retrieval quality on real queries, and adding graph, feedback learning and RVF features as each one earns its place. Installation commands, benchmarks and the full feature inventory are in the RuVector technical guide: github.com/ruvnet/ruvector.

signals.excerpt:
TorchTPU is now open source: Run native PyTorch on TPUs | Google Cloud Blog

October 20, 2026

##### Mark Lohmeyer

##### Bill Jia

Vice President, Engineering

Today at PyTorch Conference 2026, we announced a range of new products and integrations designed to help you run PyTorch effectively on Google Cloud or in your own infrastructure. Notably, TorchTPU, our native PyTorch stack for Google TPUs, is now available as open source on GitHub. With TorchTPU, TPUs join GPUs and CPUs as a native option for PyTorch. You can now train, serve, and deploy models on TPUs using the tools you already rely on, including vLLM, SGLang, llm-d, TorchTitan, Ray, TorchRec, Hugging Face, LiteRT. Ultimately, this provides our customers choice across a broad range of workload-optimized computing options including TPUs, GPUs, and CPUs, with a consistent, open software and operational model across the full portfolio.

...

### Optimizing inference

As reasoning and agentic models scale, inference cost and latency become the primary bottlenecks in production. We’ve integrated TorchTPU into widely used open-source serving engines and paired them with Kubernetes-native fleet routing across TPUs and GPUs to help you optimize throughput per dollar.

This foundation allows developers to scale workloads across diverse hardware while minimizing the friction of platform-specific tuning. To bring these framework-level enhancements to life in production, we have collaborated with leading open-source communities and industry partners. In the sections below, we explore how these partnerships are driving breakthrough efficiency across high-throughput serving with vLLM, structured agentic execution with SGLang, and large-scale distributed fleet orchestration with llm-d.

...

#### vLLM: High-throughput serving and memory efficiency

Developed in partnership with Inferact, the native PyTorch vLLM backend on TorchTPU enables developers to deploy open-weight models directly on TPUs with optimized, production-ready serving features and custom Pallas kernels. This integration supports continuous batching, quantization, and multi-chip parallelism on TPU hardware, while preserving upstream worker models, schedulers, and API servers to improve cost-performance ratios, without requiring changes to existing inference stacks.

...

#### llm-d for distributed LLM inference

To run inference engines across large fleets, we are releasing llm-d 1.0 with Red Hat, IBM, and a community of more than 500 contributors and 25 organizations. As a Cloud Native Computing Foundation (CNCF) Sandbox project, llm-d connects two open-source communities: PyTorch, where vLLM and SGLang serve models, and Kubernetes, where distributed systems run and scale in production. The llm-d router sends each request to the replica that already holds its context, using prefix-cache-aware routing. It also splits compute-heavy prefill from memory-heavy decode. llm-d 1.0 makes that ready for production with multi-tenant flow control, router high availability, stable v1 APIs, and session-aware routing for agents. On Google Kubernetes Engine (GKE), you can have the choice of running on either GPUs or Google TPUs, with a common llm-d endpoint, and choose the hardware that fits each workload.

signals.title: DeepInfer Explained: DeepSeek’s Open Inference Engine, Benchmarks, Specs, and Costs
signals.excerpt:
Skip to main content

DeepSeek has opened the inference engine behind V4.1-Flash. Its benchmarks show why large-scale serving needs specialized software, while its deployment notes reveal how much infrastructure still sits around the engine.

DeepSeek released DeepInfer on October 20, 2026, giving developers access to the inference framework it says powers its production services. The practical significance is access to the engineering that turns model weights into a service: GPU kernels, expert distribution, speculative decoding, scheduling, and output constraints.

The release deserves attention from AI infrastructure teams. It also needs careful reading. The public package provides offline inference, supports DeepSeek-V4.1-Flash on specified NVIDIA and Huawei accelerators, and leaves several service-level components for operators to build. Downloading it does not reproduce DeepSeek’s hosted platform.

Our assessment is that DeepInfer’s greatest immediate value is the combination of usable engine code and unusually specific deployment guidance. The published performance curves are useful reference points. They are insufficient evidence for a universal speed advantage, a guaranteed hosting price, or a measured reduction in electricity consumption.

...

Documented support in the inspected release

| Item | Published specification | Practical implication |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Supported model | DeepSeek-V4.1-Flash; default checkpoint DeepSeek-V4.1-Flash-1017 | A targeted DeepSeek engine; other checkpoints need explicit support |
| Accelerators | NVIDIA SM100 GPUs; Huawei Ascend 950 NPUs | Check the exact accelerator target before planning a deployment |
| Operating environment | Linux, GCC 13 or newer, Python 3.12 | The documented build targets a Linux infrastructure environment |
| Platform runtime | CUDA 13 for NVIDIA; CANN 9.2 for Ascend | Backend dependencies differ |
| Distributed execution | Attention data/context parallelism; MoE expert parallelism and expert load balancing | Engine support and the recommended production topology are separate decisions |
| Generation features | DSpark, confidence-scheduled verification, asynchronous scheduling, SWA bounded replay, structured outputs | Configuration affects both speed and validation requirements |
| Reproducibility modes | Batch-invariant inference and deterministic sampling, documented for NVIDIA only | Do not assume equal feature support across backends |
| Licensing | DeepInfer: Apache-2.0; V4.1-Flash-1017 model weights: MIT | Keep engine, model, and dependency obligations distinct |

...

## What the speed benchmarks show

DeepSeek separates prefill, which processes input, from decode, which emits output. Its main README reports prefill measurements on four SM100 GPUs and decode measurements on 64 SM100 GPUs, each within one scale-up domain. The interconnect and parallel layout are part of those results.

DeepSeek’s prefill chart, reproduced from the Apache-2.0 repository. Four SM100 GPUs, 131,072-token context, 140-token decoder bounded replay. Values discussed below are approximate visual readings.

The prefill curve rises from roughly 60,000 non-cached input tokens per second per GPU at a 4,096-token batch setting to around 89,000 at 65,536. The corresponding prefill step latency increases from roughly 70 milliseconds to 730 milliseconds. Larger batches improve throughput with diminishing returns and a latency cost.

These are prefill-step measurements. They do not include every delay a customer experiences before receiving the first token: request admission, tokenization, queueing, cache lookup, network transfer, and other stages can contribute to time to first token. “Non-cached input” also matters because reusing a prefix changes how much new computation a request needs.

DeepSeek’s decode chart. Sixty-four SM100 GPUs, 131,072-token context, fixed nextn=3, and 75% per-token acceptance scaling. The fastest-user and highest-throughput endpoints are different operating points.

The decode curve shows roughly 325 tokens per second per user and 2,600 output tokens per second per GPU at eight requests per data-parallel rank. At 256 requests per rank, it shows roughly 103 tokens per second per user and 26,000 tokens per second per GPU. Those are approximate chart readings, not raw records. They illustrate a tradeoff: raising aggregate throughput lowers individual generation speed.

Do not combine the best endpoint

...

## Accuracy evaluations: what the reference scores mean

DeepInfer includes a separate offline evaluation workflow. Its stated purpose is to sanity-check that a V4.1 deployment is configured correctly. The reference scores describe model performance under that protocol.

DeepSeek-reported reference evaluations; not independently reproduced by Kingy.ai

| Benchmark | Reference Pass@1 | Evaluation design |
| --- | --- | --- |
| AIME 2026 | 99.9% | 30 tasks × 32 samples; mean sample accuracy |
| GPQA Diamond | 93.4% | 198 tasks × 8 samples; mean sample accuracy |
| HLE-Full | 42.6% | 2,500 tasks: 2,158 text and 342 image; one sample per task |

Thirty-two AIME samples do not turn this into “the model solves a problem if any of 32 attempts succeeds.” The reported Pass@1 averages correctness across samples. That distinction matters when comparing it with best-of-many or Pass@k results.

Generation writes raw outputs to disk; scoring runs separately. The default scoring path uses an LLM judge. Rule-based scoring is available for AIME and GPQA, while HLE requires the LLM judge in this harness. Complete dataset coverage is a requirement for a valid Pass@1 figure. A paid external judge may add evaluation cost.

...

## The production deployment is much larger than the engine

The deployment notes recommend small expert-parallel groups for prefill and wide groups of 64–128 GPUs for decode. DeepSeek describes 64 prefill GPUs plus 64 decode GPUs as its smallest efficient deployment unit under the recommended layout. This is an efficiency recommendation for that production design, not a statement that every offline experiment requires 128 GPUs.

The surrounding cache system is substantial. DeepSeek describes roughly 100 PiB of SSD storage, three-day cache retention for agent traffic, and seven days for chatbot traffic. Its suggested storage server has 20 drives of 30.73 TB each and at least 40 GB/s read and 5 GB/s write throughput. These figures describe its production design and recommendations, rather than dependencies automatically provisioned by the public repository.

Why devote so much infrastructure to old context? An agent repeatedly reuses instructions, repository content, and conversation history. A cache hit can avoid processing that prefix again. DeepSeek’s design separates storage from compute so a prefill machine can reuse a prefix without being tied to the machine that originally processed it.

The public README explicitly excludes the complete KV cache system, vision/prefill/decode disaggregation service, and load balancing across data-parallel replicas. The Q&A explains their design but says cache management and load balancing remain coupled to internal infrastructure and are not yet fully open-sourced. Internal retention policies are therefore not built-in guarantees for a fresh DeepInfer deployment.

signals.excerpt:
October 19, 2026 

# Models That Use Tools

Archipelag.io now ships with a chat harness: models on the network can call tools, in the web chat, through the OpenAI-compatible API, from the SDKs and the CLI, and on phone Islands too.

 Raffael Schneider · 5 min read

Ask a small language model what 17.5% of 2,340 is and it will answer with total confidence and, often enough, the wrong number. Ask it what day it is and it will guess. Neither is a flaw you can train away in a model that fits on a laptop. What you can do is let it ask for help.

That’s what shipped this week. Every chat on Archipelag.io can now use tools: the model decides it needs a calculator, a clock or a lookup, says so in a structured way, gets the result back, and only then answers. It works in the web chat, through the API, from the SDKs and the CLI, and on desktop, server and phone Islands alike.

...

The built-in tools are deliberately plain:

- calculate: arithmetic, through a small expression parser (no `eval`, ever).
- current_time: the date and time, in UTC or at any UTC offset.
- search_cargos: looks up which models the network offers, so you can ask the chat which model is best for your task.
- generate_image: when an image Cargo is available, the chat model can hand off a picture request to it, and the image appears in the conversation.

...

## Your own tools, through the API

The built-ins are for the web chat. The real point is the API, which speaks the same `tools` and `tool_calls` format as OpenAI’s Chat Completions, streaming included. If your code already talks to an OpenAI-compatible endpoint, you change the base URL and your existing tool definitions just work.

The Python and JavaScript SDKs (0.2.0) wrap the whole loop. Write a function, mark it as a tool, and the SDK handles the back-and-forth until the model has its answer:

```python
from archipelag import Client, tool

@tool
def stock_level(sku: str) -> int:
    """How many units of a product are in the warehouse."""
    return warehouse.count(sku)

client = Client(api_key=...)
result = client.run_agent(
    [{"role": "user", "content": "Do we have enough SKU-1142 for an order of 40?"}],
    tools=[stock_level],
)
print(result.content)

```

Your function runs on your machine. The Island that runs the model only ever sees the tool’s name, its description, and the result you choose to send back. It never gets your database, your files or your credentials, which matters on a network where the computer doing the thinking belongs to someone else.
